performers: Artur Schnabel, piano; London Symphony Orchestra, Malcolm Sargent
intro: Mozart begins with a quiet string march, then lets the piano slip in, pause and trill above the returning tune. Artur Schnabel plays with Malcolm Sargent and the London Symphony Orchestra, and supplies his own first-movement cadenza.

sections.label: A · A quiet march in strings
sections.mNote: Woodwinds answer before the full orchestra joins

sections.label: A′ · Piano trill above the march
sections.mNote: The soloist adds new themes to the orchestra’s opening

sections.label: Link · The orchestra takes over
sections.mNote: G major cadences lead to a quieter string continuation

sections.label: Dev · A new piano tune
sections.mNote: A minor-key melody opens into rapid keyboard runs

sections.mNote: C major returns with the opening tune

cues.title: A march on tiptoe
cues.text: The strings begin a quiet march in C major, with short, separated notes. Woodwind replies and fuller orchestral phrases follow. The piano waits while Mozart supplies it with tunes, rhythms and several ways of answering.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, I, pp. 1–6. Hannah Chan-Hartley describes the orchestral march and wind replies: https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/36107.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mozart at the Burgtheater
cues.text: Vienna, 10 March 1785: Mozart plays this concerto at the Burgtheater in a concert for his own benefit. The advertisement also promises improvisation on a fortepiano fitted with a large pedal keyboard. The evening puts both his hands and his feet to work.
cues.evidence: Hannah Chan-Hartley, National Arts Centre programme note, quotes the concert advertisement and documents the première: https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/36107. The pedal keyboard was advertised for improvisation.

cues.title: A trill above the march
cues.text: The piano slips into the woodwinds’ conversation, runs up to a pause, then holds a trill while the strings recover their march. The soloist has arrived without taking the tune away from everyone else.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, I, bars 70–83, p. 6. Chan-Hartley describes the fermata, flourish and trill above the orchestral theme.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: G minor before G major
cues.text: The piano’s solo exposition takes a detour into G minor. Chromatic scales lead out of it towards a flowing G major tune. Mozart saves this change of mood for the soloist; the orchestra’s opening has kept it in reserve.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, I, pp. 8–9. The minor-mode detour and ensuing new melody are discussed by Chan-Hartley, National Arts Centre.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Studio 1, 12 January 1937
cues.text: Artur Schnabel, Malcolm Sargent and the London Symphony Orchestra record the concerto on 12 January 1937 in Abbey Road’s Studio 1, with Lawrance Collingwood producing. The same booking, begun on 9 January, also covers the F-major Concerto, K. 459.
cues.evidence: London Symphony Orchestra discography, session 0158 (Abbey Road Studio 1, 9 and 12 January 1937; K. 467 matrices 2EA 4604–11), PDF p. 289: https://londonso-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2024/08/Discography-August-2024.pdf#page=289 The transfer’s own description gives the same date: https://archive.org/details/Mozart.PianoConcertoNo.21

cues.title: The orchestra answers in G
cues.text: The piano’s closing trill hands the phrase to the orchestra. Winds, brass and strings confirm G major, then the strings carry on more quietly. The soloist rests before returning with another new melody.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, I, bars 194–221, pp. 14–15.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Another tune for the piano
cues.text: The development begins with a new, melancholy piano phrase, lightly accompanied by strings. Soon the soloist is running through rapid figures against held orchestral notes. Mozart keeps finding fresh things for the keyboard to say.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, I, from bar 222, pp. 15–19; Chan-Hartley identifies the new development theme.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The march comes home
cues.text: The strings recover the opening march in C major. When the piano rejoins, its entrance overlaps other statements of the march’s first few notes. The returning tune passes from player to player before the soloist moves on.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, I, recapitulation from bar 274. The overlapping entries at the piano’s return are described by Chan-Hartley.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Four discs for one concerto
cues.text: HMV issues the concerto in November 1937 on four discs, DB 3099–3102, eight sides in all. The first movement takes four, the last of them carrying Schnabel’s cadenza; the Andante and the finale take two each.
cues.evidence: John Bolig, His Master’s Voice Double-Sided Celebrity Recordings, pp. 505–506 (DB 3099–3102, first movement “Part 4 – Cadenza by Artur Schnabel”): https://www.examenapium.it/cs/biblio/Bolig2020.pdf#page=530 The November 1937 issue date is from the LSO discography, session 0158: https://londonso-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2024/08/Discography-August-2024.pdf#page=289

cues.title: Pleased without knowing why
cues.text: Writing to his father on 28 December 1782, Mozart describes his earlier concertos as a middle way between too hard and too easy. There are pleasures for connoisseurs, yet everyone else must be satisfied too, “without knowing why”.
cues.evidence: Mozart to Leopold Mozart, Vienna, 28 December 1782, Bauer–Deutsch 715, lines 10–14. Our translation of the German; the letter concerns the earlier subscription concertos: https://dme.mozarteum.at/DME/objs/raradocs/transcr/pdf/BD_715.pdf.

cues.title: Schnabel writes his own
cues.text: The orchestra stops on an unfinished cadence and leaves Schnabel alone. This cadenza is his own composition. Mozart’s full score supplies the opening in which it belongs, then waits for the soloist to lead back to the orchestra.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, I, p. 29, marks the cadenza. John Bolig’s HMV discography attributes it to Artur Schnabel in the K. 467 entry: https://www.examenapium.it/cs/biblio/Bolig2020.pdf#page=530.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The orchestra tiptoes out
cues.text: The orchestra resumes the written close in C major. Its firm opening phrases gradually shrink to a quiet ending, recalling the restraint of the first string march.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, I, pp. 29–30; the quiet close is also described by Chan-Hartley, National Arts Centre.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A trill meets the march
transitions.from: A · A quiet march in strings
transitions.to: A′ · Piano trill above the march
transitions.how: Quiet wind phrases lead into the piano’s first solo. The keyboard runs up to a fermata, then sustains a trill above the strings’ returning C major march. The strings have the melody while the soloist keeps the trill spinning overhead.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, I, bars 70–83, p. 6.

transitions.title: A G major orchestral answer
transitions.from: A′ · Piano trill above the march
transitions.how: The piano’s trill leads into the G major tutti. Winds, brass and strings take over the cadence while the soloist rests. The full orchestra then subsides into a quieter string continuation that leads towards the next solo.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, I, bars 194–221, pp. 14–15.

transitions.title: A new melody in E minor
transitions.how: The strings and woodwinds grow quiet after the orchestral bridge. The piano begins a new melody in E minor, with only light string support. The accompaniment soon drops out, leaving the soloist to extend the phrase into running notes.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, I, bars 216–230, p. 15.

transitions.title: G holds beneath the piano
transitions.how: The piano’s rapid figures continue over sustained strings and wind chords. G in the bass prepares C major. The soloist then falls silent as the strings recover the opening march, with the woodwinds answering again.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, I, bars 264–280, pp. 19–20.

transitions.title: C major above a waiting G
transitions.how: The orchestra reaches a C major chord with G in the bass and holds it under a fermata. This cadential six-four leaves the resolution waiting. Schnabel takes over alone for his own cadenza before the orchestra can finish the phrase.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, I, p. 29. Cadenza attribution: John Bolig, HMV discography, K. 467 entry, https://www.examenapium.it/cs/biblio/Bolig2020.pdf#page=530.

transitions.title: The orchestra completes the cadence
transitions.how: The piano’s cadenza leads back to the written orchestral close in C major. Winds and strings resume together, with brass and timpani reinforcing the fuller phrases. The final page reduces the sound to a quiet cadence.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, I, pp. 29–30.

source.title: Mozart, K. 467, full score: Breitkopf & Härtel, 1878; Broude reprint, plate 422
source.locator: I. Allegro maestoso, printed pp. 1–30: orchestral opening, solo entries, development, recapitulation and cadenza.

timeline.note: The strings begin the quiet march; winds and brass wait for their replies.
Strings and winds exchange phrases, with brass and timpani reinforcing the fuller answers.
The piano enters among woodwind phrases, pauses, then trills above the strings’ march. Trumpets join the held wind chords.
The orchestra closes in G major and continues into the bridge while the piano rests.
A new piano melody begins over light strings, which soon leave the soloist alone.
The piano runs against held string notes and answering wind phrases.
Strings recover the march in C major, with wind replies; the piano waits to rejoin.
Piano phrases return among string accompaniments and woodwind answers.
Winds, brass, timpani and strings take over the approach to the cadenza; the piano rests.
The orchestra resumes after the cadenza and gradually retreats to a quiet C major close.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Artur Schnabel (piano), London Symphony Orchestra (orchestra), Malcolm Sargent (conductor)
fields.note: The Archive description, photographed LP sleeve and orchestra discography agree. Bolig and the Schnabel chronology identify a Bechstein piano. The later sleeve uses Sargent’s title Sir; that is not treated as evidence of his title at the 1937 session.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The exact performing edition is not identified. Bolig explicitly credits Artur Schnabel with the first-movement cadenza; the consulted public-domain score marks the cadenza slot but does not contain his notes. The Archive description says that an earlier file mix-up with K. 595 has been corrected; the current file attribution follows that corrected record, not the superseded review. No bar-by-bar or aural authentication of the transfer has been made.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: LSO session 0158 distinguishes K. 467, recorded on 12 January, from K. 459, recorded on 9 and 12 January. The date is independently stated in the Archive description and the side-level discographies.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The Archive names Abbey Road Studios; the LSO register, Bolig and Schnabel chronology specify Studio 1. The recording venue is not inferred merely from the orchestra’s name.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Angel Records — Great Recordings of the Century
fields.note: This is the documented mono LP used for Bob Varney’s transfer, not the original shellac carrier. The original recording was issued by His Master’s Voice.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The photographed sleeve prints COLH 67 and pairs K. 467 under Sargent with K. 595 under Barbirolli. LSO session 0158 dates COLH67 to November 1959 and the original K. 467 issue, HMV DB3099–3102, to November 1937. This movement originally occupied DB3099 and DB3100.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Probable original-side lineage: 2EA 4604-1, 2EA 4605-1, 2EA 4606-1 and 2EA 4607-2A; first movement parts 1–4 on HMV DB3099–3100.
fields.note: Those issued matrix/take numbers are explicitly documented by Bolig and the Schnabel chronology. Their survival in this particular Angel LP transfer is inferred, not established by runout inspection or take comparison. The LP’s own matrix/runout and pressing are unknown. No original side-join timestamps are assigned. A targeted DAHR search produced no directly usable session record, so no DAHR matrix entry is claimed.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The source expressly states ‘Transfer by Bob Varney’; this credit is not inferred from the uploader account.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item was added on 19 April 2010, and the current MP3 has a later file timestamp following the documented correction. Neither is an identified analogue-to-digital transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: The source identifies a mono LP transfer but gives no cartridge, equalisation, noise-reduction, editing or speed-correction procedure. Internet Archive labels the uploaded file VBR MP3 and original; ‘original’ here means the uploaded file, not an original session master.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Mozart’s concerto is public domain under the ordinary life-plus-70 term; Schnabel’s own cadenza is also beyond that term.
fields.note: Mozart died in 1791; the consulted score derives from the 1878 Breitkopf edition. Schnabel died in 1951, giving an ordinary life-plus-70 expiry at the end of 2021 for his authorship. This is a territorial term calculation, not clearance of every modern edition or a claim about US cadenza publication history.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: territorial — EU public-domain basis: first published in November 1937 on HMV DB3099–3102.
fields.note: The LSO discography documents publication before 1963, independently of the 1937 session date. The ordinary EU 50-year sound-recording term had expired before the 2013 extension, which applies to recordings still protected at that date. This package uses that territorial basis only. US public-domain status is not established: this is not a recording first published by 1925. The Archive uploader links http://creativecommons.org/licenses/publicdomain/, but that declaration does not independently establish authority to release the performers’ or producer’s rights worldwide. The linked legal URL below is the term basis, not a Creative Commons grant.

dossier.credit: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Piano Concerto No. 21 in C major, K. 467, I. Allegro maestoso. Artur Schnabel, piano; London Symphony Orchestra; Malcolm Sargent. composer.epithet: In his operas a servant can outwit a count; in his concertos the piano can interrupt before the orchestra has finished its opening sentence.

quote.text: In an opera, poetry must simply be music’s obedient daughter.
quote.source: Mozart to his father Leopold, Vienna, 13 October 1781; our translation

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to try the finale through. This was K. 466 in D minor: restless, syncopated strings, then a piano entering with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert splendid.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart would dedicate the quartets to him.
